title: Docs: to the point. One reader per page, limits in one place, no test diaries
description:
Owner, 18 Nov 2026: the docs must be to the point and not AI slop.

Measured on 18 Nov 2026: README, docs/, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG and catalog/README come to about 394,000 words. sources.md 37,000; security.md 33,000; maps.md 31,000; ai.md 27,000; api.md 25,600; CHANGELOG 25,000; hf-propagation.md 22,000; the README 9,800, with table cells of 150 words. Every page ships inside the app under Help, so a household is handed all of it.

What makes them long (from reading maps.md, security.md and the README):
- One page written for three readers at once: the person using the screen, the developer (source paths, 'In the API', 'for developers') and the tester.
- 'What was and was not tested' sections on 30 of the 40 pages, and again in the README's Limits.
- The story of how a thing was found or fixed, with dates, in a guide rather than the changelog.
- Openings that list the page's own headings; the same caveat repeated in every section.

Rules for the rewrite:
1. A guide page is for the person using the screen: what it does, how to use it, what it does not do. A screen's guide should fit in about 1,500 words; the long ones are split by task, not padded.
2. Developer detail (file paths, API, formulas' derivations, test evidence) moves under docs/development/ or into api.md, linked once.
3. What has and has not been tested is kept in one page, by feature, and linked from the README. Pages do not carry their own copy.
4. History lives in CHANGELOG.md only. A guide says what is true now.
5. Say a thing once. Cut any sentence that could be deleted without the reader losing a fact or an instruction.

title: Radio range from a summit says 0.1-3 km: the estimate ends at the first slope out of sight
description: Found 18 Nov 2026 on the Pi's real terrain. title: Radio: licensed operators and listen-only operators, and what each may do
description:
Owner, 19 Nov 2026. Outpost should be very clear about what needs a radio licence and what does not. Two kinds of person, chosen in Settings (per household to start with; per person if the household PIN work, outpost-p0y4, brings people): a licensed operator, with callsign and licence class, and a listen-only operator.

- Every radio screen and guide says in one plain line which it is for: 'Listening: no licence needed' or 'Transmitting: needs an amateur licence', with the regulator's document it rests on and its date. Colour is not the only signal.
- For a listen-only operator, things that only make sense for transmitting (a callsign field, transmit planning in the HF planner's wording, sending a call in the Morse trainer 'for the air') are worded as learning or hidden, never presented as something they may do.
- A page in Help that lists it out: receiving APRS, aircraft and ships; listening on amateur, broadcast and time-signal frequencies; licence-free radio (PMR446, and Meshtastic on its licence-exempt band); and what needs a licence (transmitting on any amateur band, which includes sending APRS on VHF and LoRa APRS on 433 MHz).
- The law differs by country, and for some signals listening is itself restricted. Do not assume: take each statement from the regulator (Ofcom for the UK first, then the FCC), cite it, and say where Outpost does not know. Fits with outpost-qylj (band plans and licence rules by country).
- Outpost transmits nothing on APRS or any amateur frequency whichever kind of operator is chosen; being licensed changes what the screens explain, not what Outpost does. To confirm with the owner: the message board already sends over Meshtastic (licence-exempt) through the mesh link; this bead leaves that as it is.

title: APRS: show stations heard by a receiver on the map
description:
Owner, 19 Nov 2026. Receive only. A decoder (Dire Wolf on the Pi, a Mac, Windows or Linux; SoundModem on Windows; a hardware modem that speaks KISS over the network) listens to a radio through a sound interface such as a Digirig, or to an SDR, and offers packets as KISS over TCP. Outpost connects to that address and port and reads them. One or more receivers.

Owner's example: walking about with a radio that beacons its position; a radio at home (an RT95 or a UV-5R on a Digirig) hears it, and the walker appears on Outpost's map with a trail.

title: Heard on the radio: APRS, aircraft and ships on the map, listen only
description:
Owner, 19 Nov 2026. Outpost shows on the map what a radio receiver hears: APRS stations, aircraft (ADS-B) and ships (AIS), beside the positions mesh radios report (outpost-xeu3).

Rules for every child of this epic:
1. Outpost never transmits. It does not send APRS, and does not key any radio, on any of these paths. Sending is done elsewhere, by the person, with their own equipment and licence. There is no transmit setting to switch on.
2. Outpost never touches the radio or the audio. A decoder program does that (on the Raspberry Pi, or on a Mac or PC elsewhere on the network) and offers what it decoded on a network port. Outpost connects to an address and a port. No bridge and no Outpost client program on the other computer.
3. No internet. APRS-IS and the aircraft and ship tracking websites are not used, not as a source and not as a fallback.
4. Licence clarity on every screen (see the licence child): what a listener may do, and what needs an amateur licence.
5. The same shape for each source: Settings takes an address and port; the screen says connected or not and when the last packet came; a layer on the map; a list of what was heard with distance and bearing from Home and the age of the last report, saying which receiver heard it.
6. What is heard is kept until the person clears it, with clearing made easy: all of it, one source, older than a date, or one station.
7. Set-up is explained in the app, with examples to copy, for the Raspberry Pi, a Mac and Windows, for both ends: the decoder and Outpost.
8. Built against recorded packets and a stand-in server, and marked 'not yet tried with a real radio' until the owner has tried it, as the mesh link is.

Owner's own set-up, to design for: Outpost on a Raspberry Pi that is hard to reach, the radio run from a Mac or PC; other people will plug a radio or an SDR into the Pi.

Why: 72 bearings 5 deg apart make a glen a few hundred metres wide in sight 31 km out into a 2.7 km wedge, and can miss others; the outline joins the furthest ground in sight on each bearing, so a broken view becomes spikes and triangles over hidden ground; the wash is the ink colour at 7% opacity, nearly invisible, with seams between the 72 wedges.

Do:
1. Calculation: 720 bearings (0.5 deg), ground every 50 m near (to 25 km), 100-250 m beyond; measure on the Pi (aim: a few seconds), keep answers as now. Consider sending the viewshed compactly (runs per bearing as now, or a small raster) rather than thousands of points.

3. 4. Words: share of the ground in sight within 10/25 km, the furthest in sight with its direction ('31 km to the north-east, along the glen'), not 'on most bearings'.

title: Server stalls for 5-10 s at a time while a large move writes to the Pi's SD card
description: During the 7.9 GB move of the map data to Internal storage on the Pi (SD card), /api/health once took 5 s and /api/jobs gave no answer within 10 s; with nothing running every probe answered in 10-90 ms. The copy and hash are async streams, so the likely cause is SQLite's synchronous writes (WAL fsync on the main thread) waiting on an SD card saturated by the copy's writeback. Not confirmed. To check: measure event-loop delay during a large move; consider throttling transfer writes, fsync of the copy in steps, or fewer progress writes while a transfer runs.
notes: Root cause confirmed 18 Nov 2026 on the Pi: during a large write to the SD card (ext4, data=ordered, default vm.dirty_ratio=20% of 8 GB, about 1.6 GB may sit unwritten), Node's main thread blocks in pwrite64 from SQLite (state D, wchan do_get_write_access: waiting on the jbd2 journal, which must first flush the big file's ordered data). 2.4 GB written with dd while making a DB write each second: worst DB write 5.6 s (1.1 GB dirty). With vm.dirty_bytes=64 MB / background 16 MB: worst 1.4 s. With the writer calling fdatasync every 16 MB (default kernel settings): worst 0.33 s, health never over 43 ms, same total time (58 s vs 53 s; the default's 31 s was data still in memory). Fix: in Outpost's own large writers (collection move copy in collections/transfer.ts, the HTTP download fetcher, map region extract, P.533 maps, imagery), fdatasync the target every 16 MB; optionally also set vm.dirty_bytes in deploy/pi/install.sh.
close_reason: Fixed: large writes fdatasync every 16 MB (core/synced-write.ts). Real move of 857 MB onto the Pi's SD card: worst health 0.09 s (was 5-10 s).

title: Games: a settlement to build and run, with resources, production chains and workers
description:
Owner, 20 Nov 2026. He asked for an idle factory simulator, a mini city builder and a small resource-management or factory simulation, and suggested they be one game; he likes planned-economy builders where nothing appears from nowhere. One original game, with its own name, setting and look, that combines them. Not a recreation of any existing game.

The idea: a small settlement on a grid. Raw materials are gathered (wood, stone, clay, grain, water, later coal and ore), turned into goods by workshops (planks, bricks, flour, bread, tools), moved by hand, cart or track, and used to build and to keep people fed, housed and warm. Everything is made from something and carried from somewhere: a bakery with no flour bakes nothing, and a quarry with no road fills up.

- Three layers, built in this order so each is playable alone: (1) production chains: place buildings, link them, watch stocks and flows, find the bottleneck; (2) the settlement: housing, workers who must live within reach of work, food and fuel through the seasons, power and water; (3) trade and growth: sell a surplus, buy what the land lacks, unlock larger works.
- Runs while you are away, like the Allotment: it keeps producing at a steady rate when closed and is caught up when opened, with a cap so that leaving it a month does not break it. Nothing dies and nothing is lost by being away; shortages pause things, they do not destroy them (the Allotment's rule).
- The same settlement for the household on every device, kept on the server as the Allotment is (apps/server/src/modules/games/allotment.ts), or one each: decide when designing.
- It should quietly teach real things, as the Allotment teaches real sowing months: what a household or a village actually uses in a day (water, food energy, fuel, electricity), from the figures Tools, Supplies and Power already hold with their sources. A place where the numbers are true is more interesting than one where they are made up.
- Readable, not fiddly: a clear view of each building's inputs, outputs and what it is waiting for; a ledger of every stock and its rate; flows drawn as lines whose width is the amount. Lists before decoration. Works on a phone.
- Disk size: the owner asked. Drawn in code like every game here, with no image or sound files, so it adds a small amount of script and data and nothing else; state the size once built.
- No money to buy, no timers to pay past, no nagging: it is a game for a power cut.
- This is the largest game by far; build layer 1 and play it before starting layer 2. Simulation rules in a pure module with tests, as engine.ts is for Draughts.
- A card on the Games page, README row, a section in docs/games.md written to outpost-5da.1's rules.
notes:
Owner, 20 Nov 2026, a firm rule for the design: if I leave it, nothing bad happens. It must not be designed to keep people playing; it grows if they do play.

What that rules out: anything that gets worse while the game is closed (decay, starvation, unrest, breakdowns, raids, debts, lost stock); streaks, daily rewards and anything that is lost by missing a day; timers that count down to a loss; reminders, badges or counts that call the player back; rewards sized to how often the game is opened; shortages or events that arrive while away.

What it means in practice: time away can only help or do nothing. Production while closed carries on up to the cap and then simply stops, with the stock safe. A settlement left for a week, a month or a year is found exactly as sound as it was left, with whatever was made in the meantime waiting. Growth comes only from what the player chooses to build. Coming back needs no catching up and no apology: no 'while you were away' list of problems.

Test it: a test that advances the clock by a day, a month and a year with no input and asserts that no stock, building, person or score is lower than before. Say this rule on the game's page, in a line, so the player knows they can leave it.

title: Tools: a ration calculator (kcal a day, how long food lasts, what to store)
description:
Owner, 19 Nov 2026. Tools has water calculators; there is no ration calculator. Supplies already does the sums from entered stock (days of food by energy, each person's daily figure from Public Health England's table, energy per food from USDA FoodData Central, what to buy for a target). This is a calculator in Tools that answers ration questions without entering stock first, and reuses that code and data.

1. Stretch what you have: so many kcal (or a list of foods) and so many people: how long it lasts at full, three-quarter and half rations, with the date each runs out.
2. Plan from nothing: people and days give the energy needed, then amounts of chosen staples (rice, beans, oil and so on) that make it up, with weight and rough bulk to store or carry.
3. Adjust the daily figure for cold, heavy work, pregnancy and breastfeeding, children and older people, each adjustment from a published source.
4. More than energy: protein at least, from the USDA data Supplies already holds, and a plain warning when a ration is nearly all one food.
5. Share out a common stock by each person's need, not an equal split, as a daily amount per person.
6. 'Use my supplies' fills it from Supplies, so the two agree; the household comes from Supplies too.

As every calculator: the answer as you type, and under 'How this is worked out' the formula, its source with the date it was read, and the range it holds for. Prints.

Care: reduced rations are where this could do harm. Every reduced figure and every adjustment comes from a named body (check the Sphere standard's planning figure of 2,100 kcal a person a day, and UK guidance, before using either); nothing is invented. The screen says it is a planning aid and gives no medical or dietary advice, and names who should not be put on a reduced ration by a calculator (children, pregnant women, people who are ill).

- Time matters: four seconds of clock error is about a nautical mile of longitude. Link the radio time signals in Frequencies to listen to, and the server clock check (outpost-d9h9).

title: Map: estimated radio range from any point (a hilltop, a planned site), using the repeaters' range code
description:
Owner, 18 Nov 2026. Use case: choose a place on the map (often a hill, where someone would set up a radio) and see how far a radio there could reach, drawn as the same estimated-range outline a repeater gets.

How: reuse what the repeaters use. GET /api/maps/sight-range (at, aerial, station) already works out, bearing by bearing, how far a station stays in sight of an aerial over the installed terrain; the repeaters' map draws that as an outline. Offer it for any point: from a long press or a found place ('Estimated radio range from here'), from the line-of-sight tool's point A, and from a saved place.

Inputs, with sensible defaults and said plainly: the height of the aerial above the ground at the point (default: held in the hand, about 1.5 m; or on a mast), and the height of the other station's aerial (default: another handheld, 1.5 m; or a car, or a base station on a mast). Where the point is a summit, say so in the result.

Wording: this is not a circle and not a promise. Call it 'Estimated range' as the repeaters do, and say what it is in one line: the ground a radio at this point can see over the terrain, for the heights given; radio often reaches less (power, the band, woods and buildings) and sometimes more (reflections). Show it as the terrain-shaped outline (it is not round: a hill blocks one side), with the furthest and nearest distances. No terrain installed: say heights need terrain, as the height readout does, rather than drawing a plain circle that looks like an answer.

Not: power or band in the estimate (line of sight only, as for repeaters), until propagation is joined to it. Works anywhere in the world where terrain is installed.
notes: Owner, 18 Nov 2026: start it from the map's own menu for a point: a long press on a phone or tablet, a right-click with a mouse (the same menu that offers Save a place, Measure, Draw and the Sun times), as an item such as 'Estimated radio range from here'.
